clue.text: Go past building that's quiet just for now

indicators.note: building means constructing, so the letters of these two words are put together in a new order

parts.note: P is piano, the musical direction for quiet

explanation.surface: A temporary quiet structure passed on the way somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'building' rearranges GO PAST into STOPGA; P for quiet goes at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A stopgap is a temporary measure that serves only until something permanent arrives.

clue.text: Quarrelling in street commonplace

parts.note: rife means widespread or commonplace

explanation.surface: Arguing in the street is an everyday occurrence.
explanation.definitionFit: Strife is conflict and discord, the state of people fighting or arguing.

clue.text: Choice of brew after first love gets promoted

indicators.note: in a down answer promoted means moved higher, so the first O is moved up the word

parts.note: a potion is a brewed drink, often a magic one
love is zero in tennis scoring, and here it is the first of the two Os in the brew

explanation.surface: Choosing a love potion after your first love wins promotion.
explanation.walkthrough: In POTION the first O 'gets promoted' to the top, making OPTION.
explanation.definitionFit: An option is one of the things you may choose between, a choice.

clue.text: Partner's life Grindr ruined

indicators.note: ruined means wrecked, so the letters of the two words are scrambled

explanation.surface: Someone's partner has had their life wrecked by the dating app Grindr.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruined' rearranges LIFE GRINDR.
explanation.definitionFit: A girlfriend is a romantic partner in a relationship.

clue.text: Flipping Dua Lipa's eating what?

indicators.note: Flipping says the hidden letters are read backwards
Dua Lipa's eating means the words are taking food in, so the letters sit inside them

explanation.surface: An exasperated 'What on earth is Dua Lipa eating?'
explanation.walkthrough: The draft left the hiding unsignalled: 'eating' is the container indicator, so the whole clue is the definition. 'Flipping' looks like an expletive but reverses UALIP.
explanation.definitionFit: Pilau is a spiced rice dish, so it answers the question of what is on the singer's plate.

clue.text: Recorded in parts with little enthusiasm

indicators.note: parts is used as a verb, meaning splits open, so the word in goes into the middle of the other piece

parts.note: a muted response is one given with little enthusiasm

explanation.surface: Someone noted down bits of a meeting half-heartedly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'parts' is a verb here, meaning splits open, not the noun it seems.
explanation.definitionFit: To minute a meeting is to write up its official record, so minuted means written down formally.

clue.text: Mammal on metro upset me

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An animal on the underground train upset me.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' rearranges ON METRO ME.
explanation.definitionFit: Monotremes are egg-laying mammals, such as the platypus and echidna.

clue.text: Almost managed to climb over fence at back

indicators.note: over means covering, so the reversed word goes round the last letter of fence
in a down answer climbing means going upwards, so the word for managed is read backwards

parts.note: to run something is to manage it, so ran is managed

indicators.note: at back means the last letter of fence

explanation.surface: Someone nearly climbed over the fence at the back.
explanation.walkthrough: RAN made 'to climb' gives NAR, which goes 'over' E, the letter 'at back' of fence.
explanation.definitionFit: Near can mean almost, as in a near disaster.

clue.text: Instruction to code-breaker on the outside

indicators.note: on the outside means the code-breaker's name goes round the word to

parts.note: Alan Turing was the British mathematician who broke wartime German codes at Bletchley Park

explanation.surface: Orders to a code-breaker working on the outside.
explanation.walkthrough: TURING goes 'on the outside' of TO.
explanation.definitionFit: Tutoring is teaching, giving lessons or instruction to a pupil.

clue.text: Urgently holding court right away

indicators.note: holding means containing, so the abbreviation for court goes inside

parts.note: direly means desperately, urgently

explanation.surface: Someone is urgently taking a case to court at once.
explanation.walkthrough: DIRELY is 'holding' CT.
explanation.definitionFit: Directly can mean immediately, without delay.

clue.text: Old paintings lacking top grade frames — gold one's a Turner

indicators.note: frames means surrounds, so what is left of the paintings goes round the letter for old
lacking means going without, so the letter for the best grade is removed

parts.note: art is a collective word for paintings
A is the top grade in exams
OR is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: Old Master paintings in gold frames, one by J.M.W. Turner.
explanation.walkthrough: ART 'lacking' A leaves RT, which 'frames' O to give ROT; then OR. 'Turner' wants to be the painter, but here it just means something that turns.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotor is the spinning part of a machine such as a helicopter or turbine, so it is literally something that turns.

clue.text: Old house in road actors initially rented

indicators.note: in places the cast of actors inside the word for road

parts.note: a lane is a narrow road
the cast is the set of actors in a production

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the first letter of rented is used

explanation.surface: An old house on a street where actors once rented rooms.
explanation.walkthrough: CAST goes 'in' LANE to make LANCASTE, and the R from 'initially' rented ends it. The house is a royal dynasty, not a building.
explanation.definitionFit: The House of Lancaster was a royal dynasty that ruled England in the fifteenth century, the red rose of the Wars of the Roses.

clue.text: Court calls solely for judges

parts.note: on a tennis court, line judges make these calls when a server's foot strays over the baseline; solely puns on the sole of the foot

explanation.surface: It sounds like a legal point: only judges may summon the court.
explanation.walkthrough: Court and judges suggest a courtroom, but this is a tennis court and its line judges; 'solely' hints at the soles of the feet.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis a line judge calls a fault when the server steps on or over the baseline before hitting the ball.

clue.text: Invalid reported danger in river

indicators.note: reported means spoken of, so the word is taken by its sound rather than its spelling

parts.note: a crock is British slang for an old, sickly or broken-down person

explanation.surface: A sick person reported that the river was dangerous.
explanation.walkthrough: CROCK, British slang for an invalid, sounds the same as CROC. 'Invalid' looks like an adjective meaning not valid.
explanation.definitionFit: A crocodile lurking in a river is a classic threat to swimmers and anyone wading across.

clue.text: Bad storm and hail round east with temperature remaining constant

indicators.note: round means surrounding, so the scrambled letters go round the letter for east
bad means faulty, so the letters of the two words are scrambled

parts.note: E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: A weather report: bad storms and hail from the east, though temperatures holding steady.
explanation.walkthrough: The long definition reads like more weather forecast, but it is a physics term.
explanation.definitionFit: Isothermal is the physics term for a process happening at an unchanging temperature.

clue.text: See 17
Was suspicious — something fishy about Test cricketer

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the fish goes round the cricketer

parts.note: a smelt is a small fish
Brian Lara is the West Indies batsman who played in Test matches, international cricket

explanation.surface: Someone suspected the Test cricketer was up to something fishy.
explanation.walkthrough: SMELT goes 'about' LARA. 'Something fishy' looks like a crime, but it is a fish. The clue gives the past tense where the phrase is present.
explanation.definitionFit: To smell a rat is an idiom meaning to suspect that something is wrong.

clue.text: Wives (not Vlad's) went on about comparatively recent settlements

indicators.note: about means in a different order, so the remaining letters are rearranged
not means without, so the setter's words are removed from wives

parts.note: Vlad is the setter, so Vlad's is the setter saying I've

explanation.surface: The setter's complaint: the wives (not his) kept on about recently built towns.
explanation.walkthrough: WIVES 'not' IVE leaves WS; 'about' rearranges that with WENT ON.
explanation.definitionFit: New towns are British towns planned and built from scratch after the Second World War, such as Milton Keynes.

clue.text: Thirties' simpleton as comic film cliche

indicators.note: comic means farcical or jumbled, so the letters of the three words are reshuffled

explanation.surface: A dim-witted 1930s figure played for laughs is a stock movie cliché.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comic' rearranges THIRTIES SIMPLETON AS, all nineteen letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a well-worn movie tagline, used on posters for revenge sequels such as Jaws: The Revenge.

clue.text: Female lead at last — a new Bond producer's change for the better?

indicators.note: the leading letter of the female bird is moved to come last

parts.note: a hen is a female bird
cement produces a bond between bricks or stones

explanation.surface: A leading lady finally cast as the new Bond girl: a producer's improvement?
explanation.walkthrough: HEN with its 'lead at last' becomes ENH. 'Bond producer' looks like a film producer, but it means cement, which bonds.
explanation.definitionFit: An enhancement is an improvement, so it is a change that makes something better.

clue.text: Con government has setter going round bend

parts.note: to do someone is to con or swindle them

indicators.note: going round means turning back, so the word for setter is read backwards

parts.note: gel is something that sets

explanation.surface: A Conservative government gets the crossword setter going round the bend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Con' looks like Conservative but means swindle. 'setter' is not Vlad but something that sets.
explanation.definitionFit: A dogleg is a sharp bend, as in a road or golf hole that turns at an angle.

clue.text: Stopped being unadventurous for audition

indicators.note: audition means hearing, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: staid means sedate and unadventurous

explanation.surface: Someone quit acting dull to try out for a role.
explanation.walkthrough: STAID is heard as STAYED. 'audition' looks theatrical but means hearing.
explanation.definitionFit: Stayed means remained or stopped somewhere, as in stayed put.

clue.text: Fling books round ship

indicators.note: round means turned about, so the books' letters are read backwards

parts.note: OT is the Old Testament, books of the Bible
SS is steamship

explanation.surface: Someone hurls books around a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: OT for the Old Testament is a crossword standard for books.
explanation.definitionFit: To toss something is to throw it lightly or carelessly, the same as flinging it.

clue.text: Knackered, as Cook was before last Test innings?

definitions.meaning: knackered is British slang for worn out or broken down

definitions.text: as Cook was before last Test innings?
definitions.meaning: England batsman Alastair Cook was applauded all the way out to the crease before his final Test innings in 2018

explanation.surface: An exhausted Alastair Cook, the England cricketer, before batting in his last Test match.
explanation.walkthrough: Cook is the England batsman, not a chef: the crowd literally clapped him out to bat.
explanation.definitionFit: Clapped-out is British slang for worn out and no longer working, like an old banger of a car.

clue.text: No! Ukip leader's going to run as a Liberal?

indicators.note: run as in a stocking that runs means unravel, so the letters are rearranged
the leader is the first letter of Ukip, and going means it is removed

explanation.surface: No way! The UKIP leader standing as a Liberal candidate? UKIP is a right-wing British party.
explanation.walkthrough: UKIP with its 'leader's going' leaves KIP; 'to run' rearranges that with NO. 'run' looks like standing for election.
explanation.definitionFit: Pinko is a derogatory term for someone with left-leaning or liberal views, a pale shade of red.

clue.text: Colleague in work on left, not right

parts.note: OP is opus, a musical work

indicators.note: not means without, so the abbreviation for right is removed

parts.note: port is the left side of a ship

explanation.surface: A colleague at work, sitting on the left, not the right.
explanation.walkthrough: Port is the left side of a ship; 'on' just joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Oppo is British informal slang for a workmate or close companion, short for opposite number.

clue.text: Hounds manager that's optimistic but not around during success

indicators.note: during means within the time of, so the reduced word sits inside the word for success

parts.note: a win is a success

indicators.note: not means without, so the abbreviation for around is dropped

parts.note: chipper means cheerful and optimistic
C is circa, Latin for around

explanation.surface: A hopeful hunt manager who wasn't around when the team triumphed.
explanation.walkthrough: CHIPPER 'not' C leaves HIPPER, which goes 'during' WIN. 'Hounds' looks like a verb meaning harasses.
explanation.definitionFit: A whipper-in is the huntsman's assistant whose job is keeping the pack of hounds together.

clue.text: Complaint Democrat ignored — language!

indicators.note: ignored means left out, so the letter for Democrat is dropped

parts.note: a malady is an illness, a medical complaint

explanation.surface: A grumble the Democrats brushed off, met with a cry of 'Language!' at the swearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Language!' reads as a rebuke for swearing; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Malay is the national language of Malaysia and closely related to Indonesian.

clue.text: Sort that out, son! Most of college cuts Unite rejected

indicators.note: cuts means slices into, so the shortened college goes inside the reversed word
rejected means turned back, so the word for unite is read backwards

parts.note: to tie is to unite or join

indicators.note: most of means all but the last letter of the college

parts.note: Eton is the famous English school, Eton College

explanation.surface: A parent tells their son to handle a dispute: a college's spending cuts have been rejected by the union Unite.
explanation.walkthrough: TIE 'rejected' gives EIT; ETON less its last letter is ETO, which 'cuts' EIT. Unite is also a big British trade union.
explanation.definitionFit: To see to something is to deal with it or make sure it gets done.

clue.text: Thankful he's left school (spread fake news about Head of Geography)

parts.note: an OB, old boy, is a former pupil, someone who has left the school

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the first letter of Geography goes inside the word for spread fake news

parts.note: to spread fake news is to lie, here in the past tense

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A grateful ex-pupil who once spread false rumours about his geography teacher.
explanation.walkthrough: Old Boy is the British term for a former pupil.
explanation.definitionFit: To feel obliged is to be grateful for a favour, as in much obliged.
